Kwame had been describing his tomato beds for a long time, and the sun was dropping over the community garden in Durban. Zanele waited for a breath. "Kwame, if I've got it right, you're moving the beds to the sunny side and trying the new seeds. That sounds like a solid plan, and thank you for explaining it. I need to lock the tool shed before it gets dark, so I'll say goodnight."
Kwame paused. "Ah, yes. Go, go. Tomorrow I'll show you the seeds."
"I'd like that," said Zanele, smiling, and picked up the shed keys. Kwame beamed, lifted his bucket, and walked home in good spirits.

qa.q: Where were Kwame and Zanele when Kwame described the tomato beds?
qa.a: In the community garden in Durban.

qa.q: What was Zanele worried about while waiting for a breath in Kwame's talk?
qa.a: How to stop the talk without offending Kwame, while also caring about locking the tool shed before dark.

qa.q: What made Zanele's ending kind and clear?
qa.a: Zanele summarised the plan, thanked Kwame, and named the next thing to do, locking the tool shed, before saying goodnight.

qa.q: How might Kwame feel about the way the talk ended?
qa.a: Heard and cheerful, since Kwame beamed, agreed to show the seeds tomorrow and walked home in good spirits.

grounding: A listener gently interrupts with a summary and thanks, then names the next thing to do, ending a long talk kindly.

At the community centre reception, Sangeeta had been telling Ritu about her grandson's school play for a long stretch, from the costume to the missing prop to the teacher's speech. Ritu nodded, glancing at the clock over the door and at the chairs still stacked for the afternoon class.
At the next pause Ritu said, "So the prop turned up in the end and he got the biggest clap. That's lovely, thank you for telling me. I have to set out the chairs for the afternoon class now. Will you tell me the rest at chai tomorrow?"
"Oh, I do go on," said Sangeeta, laughing.
"Not at all. I want to hear it," said Ritu.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta telling Ritu about?
qa.a: Her grandson's school play, from the costume to the missing prop to the teacher's speech.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling while nodding and glancing at the clock?
qa.a: Interested but conscious of time, needing to end the talk without hurting Sangeeta, since chairs were still stacked.

qa.q: What did Ritu say that ended the talk kindly?
qa.a: Ritu summarised the story, thanked Sangeeta, named the next task, setting out the chairs, and offered to hear the rest at chai tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel when Ritu says "I want to hear it"?
qa.a: Reassured and welcome. Sangeeta laughed about going on, and Ritu's answer shows the interruption was not a rejection.

grounding: A listener gently interrupts with a summary and thanks, names the next task and offers to hear more later.

passage:
Dear Kiran,

You asked how I handle Lalremsiami aunty downstairs, who talks for an hour every time I pass her door. I love her, but I also have work.

Here's what I tried yesterday. She was telling me about her nephew's wedding, the caterer, the band, the cousin who fell into the flowers. When she took a breath, I said, "So the wedding was beautiful, and the band was late, and your cousin survived the flowers! Thank you for telling me, aunty. I have to get to the office now, but I want to hear the photos part on Sunday."

She laughed and patted my arm. "Go, go, beta." No hurt feelings at all.

Summarise, thank, then name what you have to do. It works.

Chaitanya

qa.q: What did the cousin fall into at the wedding?
qa.a: Into the flowers.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling while Lalremsiami aunty talked?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt fond of her but a little anxious about getting to work on time.

qa.q: Which steps made Chaitanya's ending kind and clear?
qa.a: Summarising her story, thanking her, naming the need to go to the office and promising to hear more on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami aunty respond to the ending?
qa.a: She laughed and patted Chaitanya's arm, with no hurt feelings.

grounding: Shows a listener gently interrupting a long talker with a summary and thanks, then naming what they must do next.

"So, the question was about workplace habits? Okay. I'm Sharmila, I work in HR, and I'll tell you about Rashmi.
Rashmi is lovely. But if you meet her at the coffee machine, it's forty minutes minimum. Her weekend, her neighbour, her dog's allergies. I used to stand there, nodding, with my coffee going cold and my inbox exploding.
Then I learned a trick from my old boss. When she pauses, even for a second, you summarise and thank. So now I say, 'Rashmi, that sounds like such a funny weekend, with the dog and the neighbour. Thanks for telling me! I've got a call in five minutes, so I'll run, but let's have lunch Thursday.'
She's never once looked insulted. She just says, 'Oh, go, go!' It protects my time, and she still feels heard."

qa.q: What did Rashmi talk about at the coffee machine?
qa.a: Her weekend, her neighbour, and her dog's allergies.

qa.q: How did Sharmila used to feel during Rashmi's long talks?
qa.a: Sharmila felt stuck and stressed, with coffee going cold and the inbox exploding.

qa.q: What makes Sharmila's ending kind and clear?
qa.a: Summarising what Rashmi said, thanking her, naming the next task and suggesting lunch, so Rashmi feels heard, not cut off.

qa.q: How does Rashmi react to the ending?
qa.a: She never looks insulted and happily says 'Oh, go, go!'

grounding: Shows a listener ending a long-winded talk kindly with a summary, a thanks and a named next task.

I live across the corridor from Rukmini aunty and Manoj, so I see this almost every evening. Rukmini aunty catches Manoj on the stairs and starts: the water pump, the landlord, her knee, the landlord again. Manoj listens. I don't know what goes on inside, but you can see the bags getting heavy in the hands.
Yesterday I watched him do something I've started copying. When she stopped for breath, he said, "So the pump broke, you got it fixed, and the landlord still owes you. That's so much to deal with. Thank you for telling me, aunty. I have to pick up my son from tuition now, but I'll knock tomorrow evening."
She nodded, pleased. "Yes, yes, go." No offence at all. He left, and she went in smiling. Tomorrow he'll probably knock, too.

qa.q: Who does Manoj have to pick up from tuition?
qa.a: His son.

qa.q: How does the narrator think Manoj feels during Rukmini aunty's long talks?
qa.a: The narrator senses Manoj's patience, and some strain as the bags get heavy, but isn't sure what he feels inside.

qa.q: What made Manoj's ending work?
qa.a: He summarised her story, thanked her, named the need to pick up his son, and promised to knock tomorrow, so she felt heard.

qa.q: How did Rukmini aunty feel about the ending?
qa.a: She was pleased and not offended, going in smiling.

grounding: Shows an observer watching a listener kindly end a long-winded neighbour's talk with a summary, thanks and a named next task.

Tuesday. Saurabh from the next flat caught Irawati at the lift with his theory about the water tank. Forty-five minutes later she was still nodding, and she had missed her sister's video call.
Thursday. He started again on the stairs. Irawati kept edging upward one step at a time, feeling rude and trapped the whole while.
Sunday. At the gate it began: "About the tank, the real problem is the society committee—" After a few minutes Irawati touched his sleeve lightly. "Saurabh-ji, so the real issue is the committee not checking the pipes. Thank you, that's useful. I have to go and cook now; I have guests at one." He blinked, then smiled. "Of course, of course. Go!" She walked upstairs feeling lighter, and he waved from the gate.

qa.q: Whose video call did Irawati miss on Tuesday?
qa.a: She missed her sister's video call.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel edging up the stairs on Thursday?
qa.a: She felt rude and trapped the whole time, unable to end the talk.

qa.q: Why did Irawati's Sunday ending work?
qa.a: She summed up his point, thanked him and named what she had to do next, so he felt heard and could let her go.

qa.q: How did Saurabh take being interrupted on Sunday?
qa.a: He smiled and said, "Of course, go!", so he didn't feel insulted, probably because his point had been summed up and thanked.

grounding: Shows a listener learning to end a long-winded neighbour's talk kindly with a summary, a thank-you and a clear next task.
